english.title: Aid / abet dishonest failure to disclose information to make a gain for self / another / cause / expose other to a loss
english.standardoffencewording:

english.notes:
See H8686 and H9073 respectively for the substantive offence wording and the "attempt" variation of this Standard Offence Wording document.

(i) The test for dishonesty in all criminal cases is that established in the case of Ivey v Genting Casinos (UK) Ltd (trading as Crockfords) 2017, as confirmed in R v Barton and another (2020).
(ii) The offence requires an intention of making a gain or causing loss or risk of loss; the gain or loss does not actually have to take place.
(iii) A legal duty to disclose information may derive from statute, from the implied or express terms of an oral or written contract, from the custom of a particular trade, or from the existence of a professional or fiduciary relationship between the parties such as that of agent and principal. Examples are the failure of a solicitor to share vital information with a client, or the failure to disclose information about a heart condition when applying for life insurance.
(iv) Fraud can also be committed by false representation, section 2 of the Act and H8685, and by abuse of position, section 4 of the Act and H8687.
(v) Section 12 of the Act makes provision for directors, managers, secretaries or other similar officers or person purporting to act in such a capacity to be liable to prosecution where a body corporate has committed this offence.

other.penalty:
Either way -
Summary: maximum 6 / 12 months imprisonment and/or fine not exceeding the statutory maximum.
Indictment: maximum 10 years imprisonment and/or a fine.

The maximum penalty on summary conviction is 6 months for offences committed before 2nd May 2022; for offences committed on or after that date it may be 6 or 12 months depending on the general limit in a magistrates’ court, see section 1(3) of the Fraud Act 2006 and section 224(1) and (1A) of the Sentencing Act 2020.

Time limit for prosecutions:
None

On the 12th March 2015 the limit on fines imposed by a Magistrates’ court was removed – as such, the potential fine on summary conviction in relation to an offence committed after this date is unlimited.
